CD19_B-cells.title: B cells
CD19_B-cells.what: B cells are the antibody factories of your adaptive immune response. When your body identifies a specific threat — a bacterium, a virus, a foreign protein — B cells produce antibodies (also called immunoglobulins) that bind specifically to that threat. The antibodies neutralize toxins, mark pathogens for destruction by other immune cells, and provide a long-term immune memory of the threat. B cells include several functional sub-types: naive B cells that haven't yet encountered their specific target, memory B cells that retain immunity to past threats, and plasma cells that are antibody-producing factories descended from activated B cells.
CD19_B-cells.where: B cells are produced in the bone marrow and circulate through blood, lymphatic tissue, spleen, and lymph nodes. They concentrate at lymphoid tissue sites where they encounter antigens and are activated.
CD19_B-cells.other_names: B lymphocytes, antibody-producing cells, plasma B cells (when referring to plasma cells specifically), CD19+ cells
CD19_B-cells.what_moves_abundance: What moves B cells around: - Recent illness. Acute infections mobilize B cells within days as your body builds antibody response. Signal stays elevated for weeks to months as your body finishes producing antibodies and converts some cells to memory. - Recent vaccination. Vaccinations specifically mobilize B cells to build antibody-based immune memory. Signal typically resolves over weeks to months. - Allergies.

CD4_T-cells.title: CD4 T cells
CD4_T-cells.what: CD4 T cells are the conductors of your adaptive immune response. When your body detects a specific threat — a virus, a bacterium, an aberrant cell — CD4 T cells identify it, organize the response, and signal which other immune cells need to act. They do not directly kill threats themselves; they direct the cells that do (CD8 T cells, B cells, macrophages). Without CD4 T cells, the rest of the adaptive immune system would not coordinate effectively. CD4 T cells include several functional sub-types: helper T cells that direct general immune responses, regulatory T cells that calm overactive responses (covered separately on the regulatory T cells page), and various specialized subsets that handle specific pathogen types.
CD4_T-cells.where: CD4 T cells are produced from precursors in the bone marrow, mature in the thymus, and circulate throughout the body in blood and lymphatic tissue. They concentrate at lymph nodes (where they encounter antigens presented by other immune cells) and at sites of active immune response.
CD4_T-cells.other_names: CD4+ T helper cells, Th cells, CD4 lymphocytes, T helper cells
CD4_T-cells.what_moves_abundance: What moves CD4 T cells around: - Recent illness. Acute infections mobilize CD4 cells within days. The signal stays elevated for weeks as your body finishes the response and converts some cells into memory. - Recent vaccination. Vaccinations specifically mobilize CD4 cells to coordinate the immune memory build. Signal typically resolves over weeks. - Sustained sleep deprivation.

CD8_T-cells.title: CD8 T cells
CD8_T-cells.what: CD8 T cells are the killers of your adaptive immune response. They release toxic granules directly into the target cell to trigger its death, then move on to find more targets. CD8 T cells are kept in two functional states: naive CD8 cells (covered separately on the naive CD8 T cells page) that haven't yet been deployed against any specific target, and memory CD8 cells that have fought specific threats before and are kept in reserve in case those threats return. The total CD8 count includes both.
CD8_T-cells.where: CD8 T cells are produced from precursors in the bone marrow, mature in the thymus, and circulate throughout the body in blood and lymphatic tissue.
CD8_T-cells.other_names: CD8+ T cells, cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs), killer T cells, CD8 effectors
CD8_T-cells.what_moves_abundance: What moves CD8 T cells around: - Recent viral illness. Acute viral infections rapidly mobilize CD8 cells. The signal stays elevated for weeks to months as your body finishes the response and converts some cells into memory. - Recent vaccination. Vaccinations mobilize CD8 cells, particularly for vaccines targeting viral pathogens. Signal typically resolves over weeks. - Intense exercise periods.

CD56_NK-cells.title: NK cells
CD56_NK-cells.what: NK cells are the rapid-response killers of your innate immune system. Unlike CD8 T cells (which need to be activated against specific targets), NK cells can kill on their first encounter with a threatening cell. NK cells release toxic granules directly into target cells to trigger their death, and they also release signaling molecules that recruit and coordinate the broader immune response. They are part of innate immunity rather than adaptive immunity — they do not "remember" specific threats the way T cells and B cells do, but they are always ready for action.
CD56_NK-cells.where: NK cells are produced in the bone marrow and circulate through blood and lymphoid tissue.
CD56_NK-cells.other_names: natural killer cells, NK lymphocytes, CD56+ cells, large granular lymphocytes (LGLs)
CD56_NK-cells.what_moves_abundance: NK cells decline somewhat with age but generally remain a stable fraction of the immune compartment. What moves NK cells around: - Recent viral illness. Acute viral infections rapidly mobilize NK cells. They are typically among the first immune cells to expand during viral response. - Recent vaccination. Vaccinations mobilize NK cells alongside the broader immune response. - Intense exercise periods.

Baso.title: Basophils
Baso.what: Basophils are one of the rarest white blood cells in your body, typically less than 1% of your circulating immune cells. Despite their small numbers, they have important specialized roles. They release histamine and other inflammatory mediators during allergic reactions, they help orchestrate the early-phase response to certain parasitic infections, and they contribute to chronic inflammatory states in some conditions. Basophils are part of the granulocyte family, alongside neutrophils and eosinophils. All three contain granules of pre-formed inflammatory mediators that they release when activated, but the contents of those granules and the conditions that activate them differ.
Baso.where: Basophils are produced in the bone marrow and circulate in blood. They are short-lived (days) and continuously replaced. Because they are a small fraction of circulating cells and difficult to distinguish from related cell types in some assays, they are less commonly resolved in cellular methylation research than more abundant cells.
Baso.what_moves_abundance: What moves basophils around: - Active allergic reactions. Acute allergic reactions — particularly to drugs, foods, or insect stings — elevate basophils. Signal resolves as the reaction resolves. - Persistent allergic conditions. Chronic urticaria (hives), chronic allergic rhinitis, and some chronic inflammatory skin conditions can keep basophils mildly elevated. - Parasitic infections. Less common in Western populations but can elevate basophils when present. - Some autoimmune conditions.

dendritic.title: Dendritic cells
dendritic.what: Dendritic cells are professional antigen-presenting cells. When your body encounters a threat, dendritic cells engulf pieces of the threat, process them into specific molecular fragments, and display those fragments on their surface. They then migrate to lymph nodes where they present the fragments to T cells, which coordinate the rest of the adaptive immune response. Without dendritic cells, the adaptive immune system would not know what to respond to. They are the bridge between innate immunity (which detects threats generally) and adaptive immunity (which responds to specific threats). Dendritic cells come in several functional sub-types — conventional dendritic cells (cDC1 and cDC2) and plasmacytoid dendritic cells (pDC) — each with somewhat different roles.
dendritic.where: Dendritic cells are produced from precursors in the bone marrow and circulate to peripheral tissues, where they patrol for threats. They concentrate at tissue sites likely to encounter threats — skin (Langerhans cells), gut, airways — and migrate to lymph nodes after encountering antigens. Dendritic cells are a relatively small fraction of circulating cells; most live in tissue.
dendritic.other_names: DCs, antigen-presenting cells (APCs), conventional DCs (cDCs), plasmacytoid DCs (pDCs)
dendritic.what_moves_abundance: What moves dendritic cells around: - Recent illness. Acute infections mobilize dendritic cells as your body identifies and presents the threat. Signal stays elevated for weeks during the response. - Recent vaccination. Vaccinations specifically mobilize dendritic cells to present the vaccine antigens to T cells. The signal is one of the durable signatures of a recent vaccination response. - Active autoimmune conditions.

Eosinophils_reinius.title: Eosinophils
Eosinophils_reinius.what: Eosinophils are a specialized type of white blood cell that handles threats most other immune cells are not equipped for: parasites (worms, certain protozoa) and allergic reactions. When activated, they release granules containing toxic proteins specifically designed for these targets. Eosinophils are also involved in regulating broader inflammatory responses and tissue repair, particularly in mucosal surfaces (skin, gut, airways). In modern Western populations, parasite infections are uncommon, so most eosinophil activity in routine clinical contexts reflects allergic responses rather than parasite defense.
Eosinophils_reinius.where: Eosinophils are produced in the bone marrow and circulate in blood for hours before migrating into tissue, where they may persist for days to weeks. They concentrate at sites of allergic response (skin, airways, gut) and at sites of parasite infection.
Eosinophils_reinius.what_moves_abundance: What moves eosinophils around: - Active allergies. This is the most common driver. Active allergic season (pollen, mold, pet dander, dust mites, foods you're allergic to) commonly elevates eosinophils. Signal resolves as the allergic context resolves. - Asthma activity. Active asthma flares elevate eosinophils.

Kup.title: Kupffer cells
Kup.what: Kupffer cells are the liver's resident macrophages, lining the hepatic sinusoids where blood from the gut meets the liver tissue. They make up the largest population of tissue-resident macrophages in the body. Their job is to remove particulate matter, bacteria, dying cells, and immune complexes from the portal blood before it enters general circulation. Kupffer cells are also central to liver immune homeostasis — they secrete signals that promote tolerance to gut-derived antigens and modulate the activation of other immune responses. When the liver is inflamed, infected, or injured, Kupffer cells activate, multiply, and recruit additional immune cells from the blood.
Kup.where: Kupffer cells live in the hepatic sinusoids — the specialized blood vessels that run through liver tissue. They are tissue-resident and self-renewing, with limited contribution from blood-borne monocytes under normal conditions. The plasma cell-free DNA signal from Kupffer cells comes from continuous tissue turnover and from cells dying in response to liver insults.
Kup.what_moves_abundance: What moves Kupffer cells signal in everyday life: - Recent illness recovery — viral or bacterial infection drives immune compartment shifts that resolve over weeks. - Recent vaccination — modestly increases lymphoid-lineage activity for weeks. - Active inflammation or chronic inflammatory conditions — sustained immune cell turnover. - Sleep quality and chronic stress — modest immune-compartment shifts at the population level. - Smoking — tobacco-driven methylation alterations persist years post-cessation. - Certain medications — corticosteroids, immunosuppressants, certain biologic therapies directly affect immune compartments.

Macro.title: Macrophages
Macro.what: Macrophages are tissue-resident phagocytes — large cells that engulf and digest damaged cells, dead cells, microbes, and other material the immune system needs to clear. Unlike monocytes (which circulate in blood), macrophages live primarily IN tissues, where they are positioned for rapid local response. There are two broad origins for tissue macrophages: tissue-resident macrophages that develop early during fetal life and self-renew in place (microglia in brain, Kupffer cells in liver, alveolar macrophages in lung, etc.), and circulating monocytes that migrate into tissue and differentiate into macrophages on demand. Beyond their cleanup role, macrophages orchestrate tissue repair after injury, present antigens to other immune cells (helping to coordinate adaptive immune responses), and play important roles in regulating chronic inflammation and tissue homeostasis.
Macro.where: Macrophages are produced from precursors in the bone marrow (as monocytes) that circulate to tissue and differentiate, or from tissue-resident populations that self-renew in place. They are found throughout the body — every major organ has its own resident macrophage population.
Macro.other_names: tissue-resident macrophages, M1 macrophages (inflammatory subtype), M2 macrophages (repair/anti-inflammatory subtype), CD68+ cells
Macro.what_moves_abundance: Smoking measurably elevates macrophage activity through persistent low-grade tissue damage, particularly in the airways and vascular system. What moves macrophages around: - Recent illness with tissue involvement. Infections that damage tissue (pneumonia, severe bronchitis, urinary tract infections, gut infections) elevate macrophage activity for weeks during the cleanup and repair phase. - Recent injury or surgery. Wound healing involves substantial macrophage recruitment for weeks to months. - Chronic inflammatory tissue conditions. Adipose tissue produces inflammatory signals that recruit macrophages; sustained elevation is common in obesity. - Smoking.

Bmem.title: Memory B cells
Bmem.what: Memory B cells are the adaptive immune system's institutional memory. After a naive B cell encounters its antigen and successfully activates, some of its descendants become memory cells — long-lived, ready to respond rapidly to the same antigen if it returns. Vaccines work by generating memory B cells. Childhood infections leave memory B cells that protect into adulthood. Memory B cells produce antibodies on demand when their antigen reappears, and they generate new plasma cells faster than naive cells could.
Bmem.where: Memory B cells live throughout lymphoid tissues with a circulating pool in peripheral blood. They are particularly enriched in lymph nodes, spleen, and tonsillar tissue. The blood-pool concentration is what plasma cell-free DNA and buffy-coat substrates read.
Bmem.what_moves_abundance: What moves memory B cells signal in everyday life: - Recent illness recovery — viral or bacterial infection drives immune compartment shifts that resolve over weeks. - Recent vaccination — modestly increases lymphoid-lineage activity for weeks. - Active inflammation or chronic inflammatory conditions — sustained immune cell turnover. - Sleep quality and chronic stress — modest immune-compartment shifts at the population level. - Smoking — tobacco-driven methylation alterations persist years post-cessation. - Certain medications — corticosteroids, immunosuppressants, certain biologic therapies directly affect immune compartments.

CD4Tmem.title: Memory T cells
CD4Tmem.what: Memory T cells are T cells that have already encountered their specific target and survived to be kept in long-term reserve. When you fight off an infection or respond to a vaccination, most of the activated T cells eventually die off — but a small fraction survive as memory cells, ready to mount a rapid, vigorous response if the same threat appears again. Memory T cells include several functional sub-types: central memory T cells (which return to lymph nodes and circulate; they self-renew and can re-expand), effector memory T cells (which stay in peripheral tissue and mount immediate responses), and tissue-resident memory T cells (which remain at sites of past infection). The accumulation of memory T cells is one of the natural consequences of aging. A young person's T cell compartment is dominated by naive cells; an older person's T cell compartment includes a much larger memory fraction reflecting their lifetime of immune experiences. This shift is biology, not pathology — it's the immune system gaining experience.
CD4Tmem.where: Memory T cells circulate through blood and lymphatic tissue (central memory subset) and reside in peripheral tissues (effector memory and tissue-resident subsets). They concentrate at sites of past infection or chronic immune challenge. About a substantial fraction of your peripheral T cells are memory cells; the proportion increases with age.
CD4Tmem.other_names: memory CD4 T cells, memory CD8 T cells, central memory T cells (Tcm), effector memory T cells (Tem), tissue-resident memory T cells (Trm)
CD4Tmem.what_moves_abundance: A 20-year-old has a different memory T cell baseline than a 60-year-old, reflecting normal accumulation of immune experiences over a lifetime. What moves memory T cells around: - Age. This is the largest natural driver. Memory T cells accumulate over a lifetime as cumulative immune experiences convert naive cells into memory cells. - Recent infection. After fighting off an infection, some activated T cells convert to memory.

Microglia.title: Microglia
Microglia.what: Microglia are the brain's resident immune cells. They develop from a separate embryological lineage than circulating macrophages — they arrive in the brain during fetal development from the yolk sac and self-renew locally throughout life. In healthy adult brain, microglia are continuously surveying their environment, extending and retracting fine processes to monitor synapses and tissue health.
Microglia.where: Microglia live throughout brain and spinal cord tissue. They do not circulate in blood under normal conditions. The plasma cell-free DNA signal from microglia is what crosses the blood-brain barrier — typically a very small fraction of total cell-free DNA in healthy adults, with elevation in conditions that disrupt the barrier (glioma, severe inflammation) or that drive substantial microglial turnover (active neurodegeneration).
Microglia.what_moves_abundance: What moves microglia signal in everyday life: - Recent illness recovery — viral or bacterial infection drives immune compartment shifts that resolve over weeks. - Recent vaccination — modestly increases lymphoid-lineage activity for weeks. - Active inflammation or chronic inflammatory conditions — sustained immune cell turnover. - Sleep quality and chronic stress — modest immune-compartment shifts at the population level. - Smoking — tobacco-driven methylation alterations persist years post-cessation. - Certain medications — corticosteroids, immunosuppressants, certain biologic therapies directly affect immune compartments.

CD14_monocytes.title: Monocytes
CD14_monocytes.what: Monocytes are circulating phagocytes — cells that engulf and digest debris, dead cells, microbes, and other material the immune system needs to clear. They live in the bloodstream for a few days, then migrate into tissue where they differentiate into macrophages or dendritic cells depending on what the tissue needs. When your body has an active infection, tissue damage, or chronic inflammation, monocytes are produced in larger numbers in the bone marrow and shipped to the bloodstream to deploy into the affected tissue. The expansion shows up clearly in cellular methylation patterns. Monocytes also coordinate the immune response — they release signaling molecules that recruit other immune cells, activate T and B cells, and shape whether the response stays acute or transitions to chronic.
CD14_monocytes.where: Monocytes are produced in the bone marrow from myeloid precursor cells. They circulate in the blood for a few days, then exit into tissues where they differentiate into tissue-resident macrophages or dendritic cells.
CD14_monocytes.other_names: classical monocytes, intermediate monocytes, non-classical monocytes (the three subsets), CD14+ monocytes, blood-derived monocytes
CD14_monocytes.what_moves_abundance: Smoking measurably elevates monocyte activity because the persistent low-grade tissue damage from tobacco recruits monocytes continuously. What moves monocytes around: - Recent illness. Acute infections elevate monocytes within days and the signal resolves over weeks as the infection clears. - Recent vaccination. Vaccinations mobilize monocytes as part of the broader immune response. The signal typically resolves within a few weeks. - Sustained sleep deprivation.

Bnv.title: Naive B cells
Bnv.what: Naive B cells are the surveillance arm of the adaptive immune system. They circulate through blood, lymph nodes, spleen, and tissues looking for foreign antigens they have not yet seen. Each naive B cell carries a unique antigen receptor on its surface; the body maintains an enormous diversity of these receptors so that any new pathogen, vaccine antigen, or aberrant cell will likely encounter a B cell that recognizes it. When a naive B cell encounters its matching antigen with the right co-stimulation, it activates, divides, and differentiates into either antibody-producing plasma cells or memory B cells.
Bnv.where: Naive B cells are produced in bone marrow and circulate widely. They populate the spleen, lymph nodes, and lymphoid tissues throughout the body, plus a smaller circulating pool in peripheral blood. The blood-pool concentration is what plasma cell-free DNA and buffy-coat substrates read.
Bnv.what_moves_abundance: What moves naive B cells signal in everyday life: - Recent illness recovery — viral or bacterial infection drives immune compartment shifts that resolve over weeks. - Recent vaccination — modestly increases lymphoid-lineage activity for weeks. - Active inflammation or chronic inflammatory conditions — sustained immune cell turnover. - Sleep quality and chronic stress — modest immune-compartment shifts at the population level. - Smoking — tobacco-driven methylation alterations persist years post-cessation. - Certain medications — corticosteroids, immunosuppressants, certain biologic therapies directly affect immune compartments.

CD4Tnv.title: Naive CD4 T cells
CD4Tnv.what: Naive CD4 T cells are the unactivated helpers of the adaptive immune system. After being produced in the thymus and exported to the periphery, they circulate through blood, lymph nodes, and lymphoid tissues looking for the antigen that matches their unique T-cell receptor. When a naive CD4 cell encounters its matching antigen presented by a dendritic cell or other professional antigen-presenting cell, it activates and differentiates into one of several effector or regulatory subsets — Th1, Th2, Th17, Tfh, regulatory T cells. The CD4 helper compartment coordinates the rest of the adaptive response: B cells need CD4 help to make high-quality antibodies; CD8 cytotoxic responses need CD4 help to mature properly.
CD4Tnv.where: Naive CD4 T cells circulate through blood, lymph nodes, spleen, and lymphoid tissues. The thymus produces them; the bone marrow does not. Once produced, they recirculate continuously between blood and lymphoid tissues.
CD4Tnv.what_moves_abundance: What moves naive CD4 T cells signal in everyday life: - Recent illness recovery — viral or bacterial infection drives immune compartment shifts that resolve over weeks. - Recent vaccination — modestly increases lymphoid-lineage activity for weeks. - Active inflammation or chronic inflammatory conditions — sustained immune cell turnover. - Sleep quality and chronic stress — modest immune-compartment shifts at the population level. - Smoking — tobacco-driven methylation alterations persist years post-cessation. - Certain medications — corticosteroids, immunosuppressants, certain biologic therapies directly affect immune compartments.

CD8Tnv.title: Naive CD8 T cells
CD8Tnv.what: CD8 T cells are the cytotoxic effectors of your adaptive immune response. The "naive" subset of CD8 T cells are the ones that haven't been deployed yet. They've matured in the thymus, they're circulating, and they're waiting to be activated when a specific threat shows up. When your body needs more cytotoxic firepower — fighting a virus, mounting a response to vaccination, responding to chronic immune challenge — naive CD8 T cells get mobilized and start dividing rapidly.
CD8Tnv.where: Naive CD8 T cells are produced from precursor cells in the bone marrow, mature in the thymus, and circulate throughout the body in blood and lymphatic tissue. They concentrate in lymph nodes, where they are presented with antigens by dendritic cells.
CD8Tnv.other_names: CD8+ naive T cells, CD8+ Tnv, naive cytotoxic T cells, T-naive cells
CD8Tnv.what_moves_abundance: What moves naive CD8 T cells around: - Recent vaccination. Vaccination mobilizes naive CD8 T cells as your body builds new immune memory. The signal typically peaks within a few weeks after vaccination and resolves over the following months. - Recent viral illness. Acute viral infections rapidly mobilize naive CD8 T cells. The signal stays elevated for weeks to months as your body finishes the response and converts some naive cells into memory cells. - Vigorous exercise periods.

Neutrophils_reinius.title: Neutrophils
Neutrophils_reinius.what: Neutrophils are the front-line of your innate immune response. When tissue is damaged or infected, neutrophils are typically the first cells to arrive — they migrate out of the bloodstream into tissue within hours, engulf and destroy bacteria and other threats, and release signaling molecules that recruit additional immune cells to coordinate the broader response. Neutrophils are short-lived, with a typical lifespan of less than a day after they're released into the bloodstream. Because of their rapid turnover, your bone marrow continuously produces fresh neutrophils, and the pace of that production responds quickly to immune demand.
Neutrophils_reinius.where: Neutrophils are produced in the bone marrow and circulate in blood for hours to a day before migrating into tissue or being cleared. Tissue neutrophils are short-lived and continuously replaced.
Neutrophils_reinius.other_names: PMN (polymorphonuclear leukocytes), granulocytes (neutrophils are one type of granulocyte; the others are eosinophils and basophils), polys, segs
Neutrophils_reinius.what_moves_abundance: Smoking measurably elevates neutrophil activity through persistent low-grade tissue damage in the airways. Obesity is associated with mild persistent neutrophil elevation through metabolic inflammation pathways. What moves neutrophils around: - Recent illness. Acute bacterial infections elevate neutrophils within hours and the signal resolves over days to a couple of weeks as the infection clears. Viral infections produce a more variable response — sometimes elevation, sometimes depression depending on the specific virus. - Recent injury, surgery, or tissue trauma.

Plasma.title: Plasma cells
Plasma.what: Plasma cells are the antibody producers. They are terminally-differentiated B cells that have committed entirely to antibody secretion — they no longer divide, no longer respond to new antigens, and no longer carry surface antibody receptors. A long-lived plasma cell in your bone marrow can secrete antibodies for years to decades after its parent B cell first encountered the antigen. Vaccinated immunity that lasts a lifetime is plasma cell immunity. The antibodies that protect you against childhood diseases you had decades ago are produced by plasma cells still living in your bone marrow.
Plasma.where: Long-lived plasma cells live in bone marrow niches; shorter-lived plasma cells populate the mucosal immune system (gut lamina propria, respiratory tract, urogenital tract). A small fraction circulates briefly in peripheral blood during transit. The plasma cell-free DNA signal is dominated by bone-marrow turnover plus the circulating fraction.
Plasma.what_moves_abundance: What moves plasma cells signal in everyday life: - Recent illness recovery — viral or bacterial infection drives immune compartment shifts that resolve over weeks. - Recent vaccination — modestly increases lymphoid-lineage activity for weeks. - Active inflammation or chronic inflammatory conditions — sustained immune cell turnover. - Sleep quality and chronic stress — modest immune-compartment shifts at the population level. - Smoking — tobacco-driven methylation alterations persist years post-cessation. - Certain medications — corticosteroids, immunosuppressants, certain biologic therapies directly affect immune compartments.

Treg.title: Regulatory T cells
Treg.what: Regulatory T cells are part of your immune system's calming circuitry. When your body is responding to something — an infection, a stress event, an allergen — other immune cells ramp up. Regulatory T cells make sure that ramp-up doesn't get out of control and damage healthy tissue. When they're elevated, your body is doing more of that calming work than usual.
Treg.where: Regulatory T cells are produced in the thymus and circulate throughout the body in blood and lymphatic tissue. They concentrate at sites of active immune response — tumors, infection sites, inflamed tissue — to do their calming work where it's needed.
Treg.other_names: Tregs, regulatory T lymphocytes, suppressor T cells, FOXP3+ T cells (named for the gene that defines their identity)
Treg.what_moves_abundance: What moves regulatory T cells around: - Sleep quality and consistency. Disrupted sleep over weeks raises regulatory T cell activity as your body manages low-grade inflammation from poor recovery. - Sustained stress. Chronic cortisol elevation shifts regulatory T cell methylation. Acute stress events tend to resolve quickly; sustained periods of stress over weeks or months show up clearly. - Allergies. Active allergic season can elevate regulatory T cells as your body manages the immune response to pollen, dust, or other allergens. - Recent infection.

L-MPP.title: Lymphoid-primed multipotent progenitor (L-MPP)
L-MPP.what: Lymphoid-primed multipotent progenitors are bone-marrow cells that have committed away from the myeloid lineage and toward the lymphoid lineage. They give rise to the early B-cell, T-cell, and NK-cell precursors that will go on to mature in the thymus or lymphatic tissues. L-MPP is biologically downstream of MPP and biologically upstream of mature lymphocytes. When the body mounts a strong immune response that depletes mature lymphocytes, L-MPP scales up to refill the lymphoid compartment.
L-MPP.where: L-MPP lives in bone marrow. The downstream lymphoid maturation moves to other sites (thymus for T cells, spleen and lymph nodes for B cells). L-MPP does not substantially circulate; the signal in plasma cfDNA reaches blood through constant marrow turnover.
L-MPP.what_moves_abundance: What does NOT typically affect L-MPP signal in the short term: a single bad night of sleep, ordinary daily stress, occasional alcohol use, normal exercise variation. The progenitor compartment is more buffered against everyday lifestyle noise than the immune compartment is.

MEP.title: Megakaryocyte-erythroid progenitor (MEP)
MEP.what: Megakaryocyte-erythroid progenitors are the cells that give rise to your blood's two oxygen-and-clotting workforce: red blood cells and platelets. MEP descends from CMP and is committed to one of two downstream paths — the erythroid path (through erythroblast and earlier red-cell progenitor stages) or the megakaryocyte path (which produces the platelet-forming megakaryocyte cells). MEP scales up when the body needs more red cells (after blood loss, in iron-restored states) or more platelets (after bleeding, after surgery).
MEP.where: MEP lives in bone marrow. It does not substantially circulate in healthy adults; the signal in plasma cfDNA is fragments shed during active marrow turnover.
MEP.what_moves_abundance: What does NOT typically affect MEP signal in the short term: a single bad night of sleep, ordinary daily stress, occasional alcohol use, normal exercise variation. The progenitor compartment is more buffered against everyday lifestyle noise than the immune compartment is.

MPP.title: Multipotent progenitor (MPP)
MPP.what: Multipotent progenitors are bone-marrow cells that have left the stem cell state but retain the ability to produce all major blood cell lineages — myeloid (granulocytes, monocytes, megakaryocytes, erythrocytes) and lymphoid (B cells, T cells, NK cells). MPPs divide more frequently than upstream stem cells and scale up production when the body needs more blood cells. When you recover from blood loss, fight an infection that depletes neutrophils, or rebuild marrow after chemotherapy, MPPs are the cells that respond first.
MPP.where: MPPs live in bone marrow alongside hematopoietic stem cells. They do not substantially circulate in healthy adults; the signal in plasma cell-free DNA (cfDNA) reaches blood through the constant background turnover of bone marrow.
MPP.what_moves_abundance: What does NOT typically affect MPP signal in the short term: a single bad night of sleep, ordinary daily stress, occasional alcohol use, normal exercise variation. The progenitor compartment is more buffered against everyday lifestyle noise than the immune compartment is.

NeuIm.title: Immature neuron (NeuIm)
NeuIm.what: Immature neurons are progenitor cells in the neural lineage — cells that have committed to becoming neurons but have not fully matured. NeuIm cells exist in other niches including the hippocampus and subventricular zone, contributing to the limited capacity for adult neurogenesis. They are biologically separate from the hematopoietic progenitor lineage and from the OPC glial lineage.
NeuIm.where: NeuIm cells live in specific CNS-region niches — the olfactory epithelium most prominently in adults, plus the hippocampus and subventricular zone. They do not normally circulate. Their methylation signature reaches plasma cfDNA through the very small fraction of brain-derived cell-free DNA that crosses the blood-brain barrier.
NeuIm.what_moves_abundance: What does NOT typically affect NeuIm signal in the short term: a single bad night of sleep, ordinary daily stress, occasional alcohol use, normal exercise variation. The progenitor compartment is more buffered against everyday lifestyle noise than the immune compartment is.

OPC.title: Oligodendrocyte progenitor (OPC)
OPC.what: Oligodendrocyte progenitors are the central nervous system cells whose mature descendants produce myelin — the insulating fatty layer that wraps around nerve fibers in the brain and spinal cord. Myelin is what allows nerve signals to travel rapidly. Even in adults, OPCs continue to exist in the brain and contribute to ongoing myelin maintenance and the limited capacity for myelin repair after injury. They are biologically separate from the hematopoietic progenitor lineage covered by the other progenitor pages.
OPC.where: OPCs live throughout the brain and spinal cord, particularly in white matter regions where myelinated nerve fibers concentrate. They do not normally circulate. Their methylation signature reaches plasma cfDNA through the very small fraction of brain-derived cell-free DNA that crosses the blood-brain barrier — typically a tiny percentage of total plasma cfDNA in healthy adults.
OPC.what_moves_abundance: What does NOT typically affect OPC signal in the short term: a single bad night of sleep, ordinary daily stress, occasional alcohol use, normal exercise variation. The progenitor compartment is more buffered against everyday lifestyle noise than the immune compartment is.

Erythrocyte_progenitors.title: Erythroid downstream progenitors (erythroblast, Erythrocyte progenitors, nRBC)
Erythrocyte_progenitors.what: Erythroid downstream progenitors are the cells that produce your red blood cells. They sit downstream of MEP on the erythroid branch. The sequence runs MEP → erythroblast → Erythrocyte progenitors → nRBC (nucleated red blood cell, the last nucleated stage before the mature red cell loses its nucleus). When the body needs more red cells — after blood loss, after iron stores are restored in iron-deficiency recovery, or in conditions like polycythemia vera where production is dysregulated — these cells scale up rapidly.
Erythrocyte_progenitors.where: Erythroblast, Erythrocyte progenitors, and nRBC live in bone marrow. Mature red cells are the only stage that circulates in blood. The plasma cfDNA signal from this group is fragments shed during active marrow turnover.
Erythrocyte_progenitors.what_moves_abundance: What does NOT typically affect erythroid downstream progenitors signal in the short term: a single bad night of sleep, ordinary daily stress, occasional alcohol use, normal exercise variation. The progenitor compartment is more buffered against everyday lifestyle noise than the immune compartment is.

The sequence runs MEP → erythroblast → Erythrocyte progenitors → nRBC (nucleated red blood cell, the last nucleated stage before the mature red cell loses its nucleus). When the body needs more red cells — after blood loss, after iron stores are restored in iron-deficiency recovery, or in conditions like polycythemia vera where production is dysregulated — these cells scale up rapidly.
nRBC.where: Erythroblast, Erythrocyte progenitors, and nRBC live in bone marrow. Mature red cells are the only stage that circulates in blood. The plasma cfDNA signal from this group is fragments shed during active marrow turnover.
nRBC.what_moves_abundance: What does NOT typically affect erythroid downstream progenitors signal in the short term: a single bad night of sleep, ordinary daily stress, occasional alcohol use, normal exercise variation. The progenitor compartment is more buffered against everyday lifestyle noise than the immune compartment is.

megakaryocyte.title: Megakaryocyte progenitor
megakaryocyte.what: Megakaryocyte progenitors are the cells responsible for producing your platelets. Megakaryocytes are unusual cells biologically — they are very large, with multiple sets of chromosomes, and they fragment to release thousands of platelet pieces into the circulation. Each megakaryocyte produces approximately 2,000 to 5,000 platelets across its lifespan. They sit downstream of MEP on the megakaryocyte branch (parallel to the erythroid downstream branch).
megakaryocyte.where: Megakaryocytes live in bone marrow. Mature platelets circulate in blood. The plasma cfDNA signal from megakaryocytes reaches blood through the constant turnover of platelet production at the marrow level.
megakaryocyte.what_moves_abundance: What does NOT typically affect megakaryocyte signal in the short term: a single bad night of sleep, ordinary daily stress, occasional alcohol use, normal exercise variation. The progenitor compartment is more buffered against everyday lifestyle noise than the immune compartment is.

CMP.title: Myeloid commitment progenitors (CMP, GMP)
CMP.what: Common myeloid progenitors (CMP) are downstream of MPP and are committed to the myeloid lineage. CMP gives rise to GMP (granulocyte-monocyte progenitor) on one branch and MEP (megakaryocyte-erythroid progenitor) on another. GMP is the cell type that produces all your innate immune cells — neutrophils, monocytes, eosinophils, basophils, and the macrophage lineage. When the body fights an infection requiring substantial neutrophil mobilization, CMP and GMP both scale up production to support it. They divide rapidly and turn over fast.
CMP.where: CMP and GMP live in bone marrow. Like other progenitor cells, they do not substantially circulate in healthy adults. The plasma cfDNA signal is fragments shed during active marrow turnover.
CMP.what_moves_abundance: What does NOT typically affect CMP and GMP signal in the short term: a single bad night of sleep, ordinary daily stress, occasional alcohol use, normal exercise variation. The progenitor compartment is more buffered against everyday lifestyle noise than the immune compartment is.
